title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
lead: Separate object mutation, expression value, type measurement, and selecting an evaluated branch.
why: Concise syntax helps when it keeps state understandable. Updating, an unevaluated operand, and branch selection are distinct mechanisms. One rule to read everything left to right cannot explain them.
objectives: Distinguish prefix/postfix and object state from expression result.
Explain why sizeof(++n) does not increment an ordinary int n.
Keep one update per full statement.
prerequisites: Assignment, bool, short-circuit evaluation, and sizeof(type).
Types and safe ranges. Operator overloading is not required.

concepts.definition: For int, increments the object and refers to the updated object.
For int, produces the previous value and increments the object.
Checked under language rules without ordinary runtime evaluation; the simple sizeof operand is such a case.
Chooses the second or third operand for evaluation from a bool condition.

sections.title: State and result need separate columns
paragraphs: With int count{3}; int oldValue = count++; count becomes 4 while oldValue receives 3. Next, int newValue = ++count; makes count 5 and gives newValue 5. Keep separate columns for count afterward and expression result so the distinction remains visible.

-- subtracts 1 with the same prefix/postfix distinction. As standalone statements count++; and ++count; leave the same final count because the result is discarded. Choose clarity rather than claiming one form is faster for every type.

sections.title: One statement, one clear update
paragraphs: Do not combine multiple updates of one object into a puzzle. Forms such as i++ + ++i can have undefined behavior and are unsuitable prediction experiments. Our updates occupy separate full statements, with output afterward.

Range restrictions remain: ++ on the maximum signed int is not permitted merely because the notation is short. Check preconditions first. We use 3…5 safely inside range and explain dangerous boundaries without execution.

sections.title: sizeof obtains information without evaluating its operand
paragraphs: In sizeof(++count) for an ordinary int, the operand is unevaluated and count stays 5. ++count has type int, so its size equals sizeof(int). Compare with == rather than demanding one byte count on every target. This extends the types lesson with an expression rule.

Unevaluated does not mean arbitrary text is valid: sizeof(stillUnknown) fails without a declaration. The compiler needs a valid operand and type. sizeof yields unsigned std::size_t; auto bytes = ... obtains it without an unnecessary cast.

sections.title: ?: evaluates only the selected branch
paragraphs: condition ? first : second checks the condition and evaluates first if true or second otherwise. With divisor=0 it selects 0 without evaluating 12/divisor. Zero is only a demonstration default, not a complete input-error report.

Both branches must be valid expressions even though only one is selected. Language rules determine the result type; we use two int branches. We avoid mixed signs and advanced value categories. Multi-statement branches are clearer as a separate if, treated fully next module.

sections.title: Allocation policy without hidden mutation
paragraphs: requested <= available ? requested : available selects the smaller valid count. A separate assignment reduces available. Two steps expose the rule against issuing more than stock instead of mixing ++ and ?:.

First exclude negatives and values over 100. issued then lies from 0 to available and the remainder is nonnegative. Test requested=0, requested=available, and requested>available. These are distinct contract cases even if two produce the same stdout for a particular stock.

sections.title: Checking three different mechanisms
paragraphs: For ++ record prior state, result, and final state. For sizeof record count before and after plus size equality. For ?: identify the chosen and skipped branches. A final number alone often hides a wrong explanation.

The diagram is a fixed journal over 3…5. Next does not mutate a live C++ object; execution is checked in Code Studio. Retain predictions made before running so the report identifies the hypothesis actually tested.
